summary: Clarifies and updates the DANE TLSA specification from RFC 6698 based on implementation experience. It also gives guidance to implementers, operators and protocol developers who want to use DANE records.

plainLanguage.summary: DANE lets the owner of a domain say in the DNS which certificate or key its server should present, and lets a client check the server against that record. The record is only trustworthy when DNSSEC validates it. This RFC does not invent DANE. It says which of the many possible record types to use, how to change keys without breaking service, and what has to be true of the DNS underneath.

subtitle: Which DANE records to publish, how to change keys without breaking service, and what DNSSEC has to guarantee.

tldr.problem: RFC 6698 defined the DANE TLSA record, with three numeric fields that produce 24 different kinds of record. It left implementers to work out for themselves which kinds to publish, how to change keys without breaking service, and how to find the record when a domain is an alias.
tldr.mechanism: This document recommends a small set of record types, in particular DANE-EE(3) SPKI(1) SHA2-256(1) for most sites, and adds rules for certificate usage selection, for finding the TLSA record through CNAME expansion, for rolling keys over safely, and for choosing the strongest digest algorithm a client supports.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 6698 in nine specific places and gathers the operational guidance that implementers of DANE, DNSSEC and TLS needed. It also states plainly that the security of DANE rests on the security of the DNSSEC zone that signs the TLSA records.

today: RFC 7671 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2015. It updates RFC 6698, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or further updates it. The application-specific companion for mail is RFC 7672, and the guidance for combining DANE with SRV records is in RFC 7673.

sections.title: What DANE Does and What This Document Adds
sections.content:
DANE, the DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities, introduces the DNS TLSA resource record type. A TLSA record associates a certificate or a public key of an end entity, or of a trusted issuing authority, with the corresponding TLS or DTLS transport endpoint. DANE relies on the DNS Security Extensions, so a TLSA record validated by DNSSEC can be used to augment or replace the use of trusted public Certification Authorities.

Used without authentication, TLS protects a connection only against eavesdropping, through its encryption. With authentication, TLS also protects the transport against man-in-the-middle attacks.

RFC 6698 defines three TLSA fields: the first with four possible values, the second with two, and the third with three, which yield 24 distinct combinations of TLSA record types. This document recommends a smaller set of best-practice combinations to simplify protocol design, implementation and deployment. It also explains and recommends DANE-specific strategies to simplify virtual hosting, where a single Service Provider transport endpoint serves several Customer Domains, and it collects the operational guidance implementers need. Section 12 of the RFC lists the normative updates it makes to RFC 6698.
sections.plainLanguage: DANE lets the owner of a domain say in the DNS which certificate or key its server should present, and lets a client check that against the record. The record is only trustworthy when DNSSEC validates it. This RFC does not invent DANE. It says which of the many possible record types to use, how to change keys without breaking service, and what has to be true of the DNS underneath.

sections.title: The Four Fields of a TLSA Record
sections.content:
A TLSA record has four fields. The first three are numeric parameters that say what the fourth field means, and this document calls them the TLSA parameters. The fourth field, the Certificate Association Data, stores the full value or the digest of the certificate or of the subject public key, as the matching type and selector require.

The Certificate Usage field has four values: PKIX-TA(0), PKIX-EE(1), DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3). There is also a private-use value, PrivCert(255), and all other values are reserved for future specifications. The Selector field has two values, Cert(0) and SPKI(1), plus a private-use value PrivSel(255). The Matching Type field has three values, Full(0), SHA2-256(1) and SHA2-512(2), plus a private-use value PrivMatch(255).

Of the two digest algorithms, only SHA2-256(1) is mandatory to implement. Clients SHOULD implement SHA2-512(2), but servers SHOULD NOT publish SHA2-512(2) digests exclusively. The digest algorithm agility protocol of Section 9 SHOULD be used by clients to decide how to process RRsets that use more than one digest algorithm, and server operators MUST publish RRsets that are compatible with that agility.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLSA record has four parts. The first three are numbers that say what the fourth part should be compared against: whether it is a certificate or a public key, and whether the record holds the whole thing or a hash of it. The recommended hash is SHA2-256.

sections.title: Choosing a Certificate Usage
sections.content:
With PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1), validating a peer's certificate chain needs preconfigured CA trust anchors that the operators of the server and the client both trust. With DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3), no preconfigured trust anchors are needed, because the published TLSA records are enough to verify the peer's chain.

Application standards that use DANE TLSA can give more specific guidance than this document gives. They need to choose carefully which usages to support, and simultaneous support for all four is NOT RECOMMENDED for DANE clients. The reason is that an attacker who can compromise the integrity of DNSSEC only has to replace the server's TLSA RRset with one listing suitable DANE-EE(3) or DANE-TA(2) records, and that bypasses the extra checking the public CA path would have given. When all four usages are supported, the two PKIX usages offer only illusory extra security over the two DANE usages.

Designs in which clients support just DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) are RECOMMENDED, because then clients do not have to track a large, changing list of X.509 trust anchors in order to authenticate servers whose certificates come from a CA that is new or not widely trusted. The records published for a server MAY include both sets of usages when a mixture of clients has to be supported.

When the client's design is based on opportunistic security, the use of the PKIX-EE(1) and PKIX-TA(0) usages is especially to be avoided. In that model the client tries to protect the channel at the server's request and would otherwise be willing to use cleartext, so a fragile mechanism that depends on both sides happening to trust the same CA is a poor fit. If usable secure TLSA records are published, then authentication MUST succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways a TLSA record can be used, and the RFC says to pick two of them. The two that rely on a public certification authority add nothing when the DNS-based ones are also supported, because an attacker who can forge DNS records can simply publish the other kind instead.

sections.title: DANE-EE and DANE-TA in Practice
sections.content:
With certificate usage DANE-EE(3), authentication simply checks that the server's leaf certificate matches the TLSA record. The binding of the server public key to its name comes entirely from the TLSA record, and the server MUST be considered authenticated even if none of the names in the certificate match the client's reference identity for the server. That simplifies servers that host several Customer Domains, because one certificate can be associated with several domains without matching each of the corresponding reference identifiers.

With DANE-EE(3) the expiration date of the server certificate MUST be ignored. The validity of the key binding comes from the DNSSEC signatures on the TLSA record, and it is reaffirmed by continuing to publish the record and sign the zone. A missing expiration date no longer causes an outage; it only reminds the administrator that the key is probably due for rotation.

It is RECOMMENDED that most sites publish TLSA records of the type "DANE-EE(3) SPKI(1) SHA2-256(1)". The SPKI selector is chosen because it works with raw public keys and the record does not have to change when the certificate is renewed with the same key. The SHA2-256 matching type is chosen because every DANE implementation is required to support SHA2-256.

With certificate usage DANE-TA(2), the record names a trust anchor instead of the end-entity certificate, and the server MUST include the TA certificate in its TLS server certificate message unless all of its DANE-TA records are "2 0 0" records that publish the server certificate in full. The DNSSEC records for a server MAY include both sets of usages when a mixture of clients is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommended record says: this exact key belongs to this service. The client checks the key the server presents against the record and, if it matches, treats the server as authenticated. Because the binding comes from the DNS record, the certificate does not even have to carry the right name in it, and its expiry date is ignored.

sections.title: Finding the TLSA Record
sections.content:
TLSA records live at a name built from a port and protocol prefix, such as _443._tcp, plus a base domain. This document modifies the lookup strategy to prefer the fully CNAME-expanded name of the TLS server, provided the expansion is secure, meaning DNSSEC validated, at each stage and TLSA records are published for that fully expanded name. The base domain is therefore either the fully CNAME-expanded server name or the initial fully qualified name, whichever is used with the prefix to obtain the TLSA RRset.

When the application protocol has no way to locate the service other than by a CNAME, the complexity of coordinating key management between a customer and a service provider is largely removed if the TLSA records are found in the provider's domain. DANE TLS clients connecting to a server whose domain name is a CNAME alias SHOULD follow the CNAME hop by hop to its ultimate target host, noting at each step whether the CNAME is DNSSEC validated. If every stage of the expansion is secure, the final target name SHOULD be the preferred base domain for TLSA lookups. A client that fails to find a TLSA record under that name SHOULD issue the query using the original destination name.

When the base domain is the result of a secure CNAME expansion, the resulting name MUST be used as the HostName in the client's SNI extension, and it MUST be the primary reference identifier for peer certificate matching with usages other than DANE-EE(3).
sections.plainLanguage: The client has to know which name to ask for. If the domain is an alias, the RFC says to follow the alias to its final name, as long as each step is validated by DNSSEC, and to ask for the record there. If nothing is found, it falls back to the name the client originally asked for.

sections.title: Changing Keys Without Breaking Service
sections.content:
The TLSA Publisher MUST ensure that each combination of certificate usage, selector and matching type in the server's TLSA RRset includes at least one record that matches the server's current certificate chain. Records that match recently retired or not yet deployed chains will be present during a key rollover, but such past or future records MUST NOT at any time be the only records published for a given combination. This matters because not all clients support all combinations: some may not support a digest algorithm, some may support only the PKIX usages, and some may negotiate raw public keys.

The simplest case is a key rollover that keeps the same parameter combinations. The records matching the existing chain are first augmented with records matching the future keys, at least two TTLs or longer before the new chain is deployed. That lets the obsolete RRset age out of client caches before the new chain is used in TLS handshakes. The administrator can then deploy the new chain, verify that it works, and remove the records for the chain that is no longer active.

When adding or switching to a new combination of parameters, the new combinations are published for the existing certificate chain first, and only then are new keys deployed if that is wanted. The summary of safe changes says: pre-publish new associations that use the same parameters as existing records but match chains that will be deployed soon; wait for stale RRsets to expire from DNS caches before configuring the servers; remove records matching chains that are no longer deployed; and publish RRsets in which all parameter combinations match the same set of current and planned chains.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys have to be changed from time to time, and the change must not break the service. The method is to publish the new record first and let it sit for at least two cache lifetimes, then switch the server, then delete the old record. Every type of record in the set has to stay valid on its own, because a client may only understand some of the types.

sections.title: Digest Algorithm Agility
sections.content:
RFC 6698 specifies several digest algorithms but no way for the client and the publisher to agree on the strongest one they share. This section adds such a protocol, so that deprecated weaker algorithms, which may be published for compatibility with less capable clients, are avoided when possible. The protocol never avoids records with a DANE matching type of Full(0), because those do not use a digest algorithm that could be weakened by cryptanalysis.

Client implementations SHOULD implement a default order of digest algorithms by strength, and that order SHOULD be configurable. To make agility possible, all published DANE TLSA RRsets MUST conform to the requirements of Section 8. Clients SHOULD use agility when processing the peer's records, after discarding any unusable or malformed records. For each usage and selector, the client SHOULD process only the usable records with a matching type of Full(0) and the usable records whose digest algorithm it considers the strongest among the usable records with that usage and selector. In the RFC's example, a client that prefers SHA2-512(2) accepts a server key that matches the "3 1 0" or the "3 1 2" record, but not one that matches only the weaker "3 1 1" record.
sections.plainLanguage: A record can carry several kinds of hash, so that older clients still work. The RFC adds a rule for the client: throw out the records it cannot use, then keep the ones with the strongest hash it supports. That way a weak hash sitting in the same record set does not weaken the check.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The DNS TTL of TLSA records needs to be chosen with care. When an unplanned change in the server's certificate chain and RRset is required, such as when keys are compromised or lost, clients that cache stale TLSA records will fail to validate the certificate chain of the updated server, so TTLs should be short enough to limit the disruption to an acceptable duration.

The signature lifetime for TLSA records SHOULD NOT be too long. Signed DNSSEC records can be replayed by a man-in-the-middle attacker while the signatures have not yet expired, and shorter signature validity periods allow faster invalidation of compromised keys.

The security of the DANE TLSA public key infrastructure rests on the security of the underlying DNSSEC infrastructure. Under the Registry, Registrar and Registrant model, only the registrar of record can update a domain's DS record, and DNS operators are advised to set a registrar lock on their domains so that a rogue registrar cannot easily start an unauthorised domain transfer. DNSSEC-signed RRsets cannot be securely revoked before they expire, so operators should not generate signatures of excessive length: for domains publishing high-value keys a signature lifetime of a few days is reasonable and the zone can be re-signed daily, while for less critical data a couple of weeks to a month is reasonable and the zone can be re-signed weekly. Short signature lifetimes need tighter synchronisation between the primary and secondary nameservers, and they limit how long the primary server may be down, so they suit sites with dedicated operations staff. Monitoring matters too: a zone that is not re-signed in time makes the whole domain and all its subdomains bogus.
sections.plainLanguage: Two settings decide how quickly a broken key or a stale record causes trouble. The cache lifetime of the record sets how long old data lingers, and the signature lifetime sets how long forged data stays acceptable. The RFC says to keep both short, and notes that keeping signatures short means the name servers have to be kept closely in step with each other.

items.label: PKIX-TA
items.desc: The record names a CA that must appear in a chain that also passes normal PKIX validation.

items.label: PKIX-EE
items.desc: The record names the end-entity certificate, which must also pass normal PKIX validation.

items.label: DANE-TA
items.desc: The record names a trust anchor. No preconfigured CA trust anchors are needed.

items.label: DANE-EE
items.desc: The record names the end-entity certificate or public key. No preconfigured CA trust anchors are needed.

viz.caption: THE SAFE STEPS OF A KEY ROLLOVER

items.title: Pre-publish
items.text: Add records with the same parameters as the existing ones, but matching the chain that will be deployed soon.

items.title: Wait
items.text: Leave them in place for at least two TTLs so that stale RRsets expire from client caches.

items.title: Switch the server
items.text: Deploy the new certificate chain and verify that it works.

items.title: Remove
items.text: Delete the records for the chain that is no longer deployed, and keep every parameter combination valid on its own.
